items.question: "Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary, not contradictory." In the light of judicial pronouncements, examine the evolving balance between the two.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Fundamental Rights (Part III)** and **Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV)** together form the **conscience of the Constitution** — the former securing **political democracy**, the latter **social and economic democracy**. Though the framers made DPSP **non-justiciable (Article 37)**, they intended the two to be read harmoniously.

The judicial journey began with **Champakam Dorairajan (1951)**, where the Court held that in a conflict **Fundamental Rights would prevail**, prompting the **1st, 4th and 17th Amendments** to protect welfare laws. In **Golaknath (1967)** the Court declared FR **unamendable**, triggering the **24th and 25th Amendments**, the latter inserting **Article 31C** to give primacy to laws implementing **Article 39(b) and (c)**. The **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)** resolved the tension through the **basic structure doctrine** — Parliament may amend FR to implement DPSP, but cannot destroy the Constitution's basic features, and DPSP cannot override that structure. Finally, **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down the 42nd Amendment's attempt to give **all** DPSP absolute primacy over Articles 14 and 19, holding that **the harmony and balance between FR and DPSP is itself part of the basic structure**.

Subsequent jurisprudence has fused the two: the **right to education** (read into Article 21 and later Article 21A), the **right to a clean environment** (Article 21 + Article 48A) and **legal aid** (Article 21 + Article 39A) show DPSP being used to **expand and interpret** Fundamental Rights. In **Andhra Pradesh**, land-reform legislation and welfare schemes reflect the same directive spirit. Thus the relationship has matured from **conflict to complementarity** — neither is superior; each gives meaning to the other in the pursuit of justice under the Preamble.
keyPoints: FR = political democracy (Part III); DPSP = social & economic democracy (Part IV, Art 37 non-justiciable).
Golaknath (1967) → 24th & 25th Amendments; Article 31C protects Art 39(b)/(c) laws.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): basic structure doctrine harmonises FR and DPSP.
Minerva Mills (1980): FR-DPSP balance is part of the basic structure.
DPSP now expand FR — RTE (Art 21A), environment (Art 48A), legal aid (Art 39A).

items.question: "The Directive Principles are the instrument through which the Constitution seeks to build a welfare state." Discuss with reference to their classification and implementation.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Directive Principles of State Policy** translate the Preamble's promise of **justice — social, economic and political** into concrete directions for the State. Though **non-justiciable under Article 37**, they are 'fundamental in the governance of the country' and mark the transition from a **police state to a welfare state**, resembling the **'Instrument of Instructions'** of the Government of India Act, 1935.

The principles fall into three streams. **Socialistic** directives (Art 38, 39, 41, 43, 47) target **economic justice** — adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work, prevention of the concentration of wealth, a living wage and better nutrition and health. **Gandhian** directives (Art 40, 43, 46, 47, 48) reflect **grassroots self-reliance** — village panchayats, cottage industries, upliftment of SCs/STs and weaker sections, prohibition and cattle protection. **Liberal-Intellectual** directives (Art 44, 45, 48A, 50, 51) advance a **modern, rational polity** — a Uniform Civil Code, early childhood care, environmental protection, judicial independence and international peace.

Implementation has been substantial: **land reforms and zamindari abolition**, the **Minimum Wages Act (1948)** and **Equal Remuneration Act (1976)**, **bank nationalisation**, the **73rd/74th Amendments (1992)** realising Article 40, **MGNREGA (2005)** giving effect to the right to work, and the **Right to Education Act (2009)**. In **Andhra Pradesh**, the mandal-based panchayati raj structure and a range of welfare schemes carry the directive spirit forward. Critics note the absence of legal force and an illogical arrangement, yet the DPSP remain a **yardstick of governance** and a moral compass — measured at every election — that has steadily shaped India into a **social welfare democracy**.
keyPoints: DPSP operationalise the Preamble's social, economic and political justice; welfare-state ideal (Art 37).
Socialistic (38, 39, 41, 43, 47): livelihood, equal pay, living wage, health.
Gandhian (40, 43, 46, 47, 48): panchayats, cottage industries, weaker sections, prohibition.
Liberal-Intellectual (44, 45, 48A, 50, 51): UCC, environment, judicial independence, peace.
Implementation: land reforms, wage laws, 73rd/74th Amendments, MGNREGA, RTE Act 2009.
AP angle: mandal panchayati raj and state welfare schemes; criticism = no legal force, illogical arrangement.
